title: Philippians COMA Study
description: 6-week walkthrough of Philippians using the COMA method (Context, Observation, Meaning, Application) from a Reformed Baptist perspective

gospelData.title: Week 1: Joy & Partnership in the Gospel

subsections.title: Introduction to Philippians
subsections.content:
Paul wrote this letter from prison (likely Rome, around AD 61-62) to the church at Philippi—the first church he planted in Europe. Philippi was a Roman colony, and many of its citizens were proud of their Roman citizenship. Paul had a deep affection for this congregation, who had supported his ministry financially and sent Epaphroditus to care for him.

The founding of this church is recorded in Acts 16, where we see Lydia and the Philippian jailer come to faith and be baptized.

Despite being in chains, Paul's letter overflows with joy—the word appears 16 times. This week we explore Paul's greeting and his prayer of thanksgiving for the Philippians' partnership in the gospel.

subsections.title: Greeting and Thanksgiving
subsections.content: Read the passage slowly, noting Paul's affection for the Philippians and his confidence in God's work among them.

questions.question: Context: Who wrote this letter? Who was it written to? What do we know about Paul's circumstances and his relationship with the Philippian church from Acts 16 and this passage?
Observation: What words or phrases stand out? How does Paul describe his feelings toward the Philippians? What specific things does he thank God for? What does he pray for them?

Meaning: What does 'partnership in the gospel' (Philippians 1:5) mean? What is the 'good work' God began in them (Philippians 1:6), and what does God's promise to 'bring it to completion' teach about the security of true believers? How does this passage demonstrate that those whom God effectually calls, He also preserves to the end?

Application: How does Paul's confidence in God's faithfulness (Philippians 1:6) encourage you today? What would it look like for your love to 'abound more and more' with knowledge and discernment (Philippians 1:9-10)?

subsections.title: Context for This Week
subsections.content: Paul shares how his imprisonment has actually advanced the gospel. Rather than being discouraged, he rejoices that Christ is being proclaimed. He then addresses his own perspective on life and death, revealing his famous declaration: 'For to me to live is Christ, and to die is gain.'

subsections.title: The Gospel Advances Through Chains
subsections.content: Read how Paul's imprisonment became an opportunity for gospel witness.

questions.question: Context: Where is Paul writing from? How has his situation become known throughout the 'whole imperial guard' (Philippians 1:13)?
Observation: What two groups are preaching Christ (Philippians 1:15-17)? What are their different motivations? How does Paul respond to both?
Meaning: Why can Paul rejoice even when some preach Christ from 'selfish ambition'? What does this reveal about his priorities and the power of the gospel message itself?
Application: How might God use your difficult circumstances to advance the gospel? Are you able to rejoice when Christ is proclaimed, even if the messenger's motives aren't pure?

subsections.title: To Live Is Christ
subsections.content: Paul shares his inner conflict between departing to be with Christ and remaining for the sake of the church.

questions.question: Context: What is Paul facing? Why is he torn between two desires (Philippians 1:23-24)?
Observation: What does Paul mean by 'to live is Christ, and to die is gain' (Philippians 1:21)? What instructions does he give about their conduct (Philippians 1:27-28)?
Meaning: What does it mean to 'live in a manner worthy of the gospel' (Philippians 1:27)? How is suffering 'granted' as a gift alongside believing (Philippians 1:29)?
Application: If you completed the sentence 'For to me to live is _____, and to die is _____,' what would honestly fill those blanks? How can you grow toward Paul's perspective?

subsections.title: Context for This Week
subsections.content: This week contains one of the most important theological passages in the New Testament—the 'Christ Hymn' (2:5-11). Paul calls the church to unity and humility, then points to Jesus as the ultimate example of self-emptying love. He concludes with a call to work out their salvation and shine as lights in the world.

subsections.title: A Call to Unity
subsections.content: Paul appeals for like-mindedness and selfless concern for others.

questions.question: Context: What four 'if' statements does Paul make in Philippians 2:1? What do these reveal about the Philippians' experience with Christ?
Observation: What does Paul ask them to do (Philippians 2:2)? What attitudes are they to avoid (Philippians 2:3)? What attitude should replace them (Philippians 2:3-4)?
Meaning: What is 'selfish ambition' and 'vain conceit'? Why is counting others more significant than yourself the key to unity?
Application: Where do you struggle with selfish ambition or looking only to your own interests? How can you practically 'count others more significant' this week?

subsections.title: The Christ Hymn
subsections.content: The supreme example of humility: Christ's self-emptying and exaltation.

questions.question: Context: This passage is often called the 'Christ Hymn' or 'Kenosis' passage. How does it fit into Paul's argument about humility and unity?

Observation: Trace Christ's descent (Philippians 2:6-8): What did He not grasp? What did He take? How far did He go? Now trace His ascent (Philippians 2:9-11): What did God do? What will happen at His name?

Meaning: What does it mean that Christ 'emptied himself' (Philippians 2:7)? How does His perfect obedience throughout His life (active obedience) and His obedience 'to the point of death' (passive obedience) relate to the righteousness credited to believers? What does 'Jesus is Lord' (Philippians 2:11) declare about His identity and authority?
Application: What would it look like to 'have this mind' (Philippians 2:5) in your relationships, work, or church? Where is God calling you to voluntary humility?

subsections.title: Work Out Your Salvation
subsections.content: Paul calls them to obedience and gives the promise that God is at work in them.

questions.question: Context: Why does Paul say 'work out your salvation' after describing Christ's finished work? What balance is Paul presenting?
Observation: What are they to work out (Philippians 2:12)? Who is at work in them (Philippians 2:13)? How are they to live (Philippians 2:14-15)? What does Paul call them (Philippians 2:15)?

Meaning: How do verses 12 and 13 work together? If God 'works in you, both to will and to work,' what does this teach about divine sovereignty and human responsibility in sanctification? Note that we work OUT what God works IN—our effort flows from His prior and ongoing grace. What does it mean to 'shine as lights' in a 'crooked and twisted generation'?
Application: Where are you prone to 'grumbling or disputing'? How can you hold fast to the word of life and shine as a light this week?

subsections.title: Context for This Week
subsections.content: Paul highlights Timothy and Epaphroditus as living examples of the Christ-like humility he just described. Then in chapter 3, he warns against those who trust in religious credentials, using his own impressive resume to show that everything is 'rubbish' compared to knowing Christ.

subsections.title: Timothy & Epaphroditus
subsections.content: Two examples of self-sacrificing service for the gospel.

questions.question: Context: Who are Timothy and Epaphroditus? What roles have they played in Paul's ministry and his relationship with the Philippians?
Observation: How does Paul describe Timothy's character (Philippians 2:20-22)? What happened to Epaphroditus (Philippians 2:26-27, 30)? How should the Philippians receive him (Philippians 2:29)?
Meaning: Why does Paul include these personal examples right after the Christ Hymn? How do Timothy and Epaphroditus model 'looking to the interests of others'?
Application: Who in your life models Timothy's genuine concern or Epaphroditus's sacrificial service? How can you 'honor such people' (Philippians 2:29)?

subsections.title: Counting All as Loss for Christ
subsections.content: Paul's credentials versus knowing Christ.

questions.question: Context: Who are the 'dogs' and 'mutilators of the flesh' Paul warns against (Philippians 3:2)? What were they teaching?
Observation: List Paul's credentials (Philippians 3:4-6). What does he now count as 'loss' and 'rubbish' (Philippians 3:7-8)? What does he want instead (Philippians 3:8-10)?

Meaning: What is the difference between 'a righteousness of my own that comes from the law' and 'the righteousness from God that depends on faith' (Philippians 3:9)? This is the heart of justification by faith alone—an 'alien righteousness' not produced by us but imputed to us. How does this passage refute any mixture of works in our justification before God? What does it mean to 'know Christ' and 'the power of his resurrection' and 'share in his sufferings'?
Application: What 'credentials' or achievements might you be tempted to trust in? How does Paul's example challenge you to count them as loss for the surpassing worth of knowing Christ?

subsections.title: Context for This Week
subsections.content: Paul describes the Christian life as a race—pressing on toward the goal, straining forward, forgetting what lies behind. He warns against those whose 'god is their belly' and reminds the Philippians that their citizenship is in heaven. Chapter 4 opens with personal appeals for unity and the famous call to 'rejoice in the Lord always.'

subsections.title: Pressing Toward the Goal
subsections.content: The Christian race: not yet perfected, but pressing on.

questions.question: Context: How does this passage connect to Paul's desire to 'know Christ' in the previous section?
Observation: What has Paul 'not already obtained' (Philippians 3:12)? What is 'the one thing' he does (Philippians 3:13-14)? What is the prize?
Meaning: Why is 'forgetting what lies behind' essential to pressing forward? What does it mean that Christ Jesus has 'made me his own' (Philippians 3:12)?
Application: What 'things behind' do you need to forget—past failures, past successes, past hurts? How will you press on toward the goal this week?

subsections.title: Citizens of Heaven
subsections.content: A warning against worldliness and a reminder of our true citizenship.

questions.question: Context: Who are the 'enemies of the cross of Christ' Paul mentions (Philippians 3:18)? How does this contrast with the examples of Timothy and Epaphroditus?
Observation: What characterizes the enemies of the cross (Philippians 3:19)? Where is our citizenship (Philippians 3:20)? What are we awaiting (Philippians 3:20-21)?
Meaning: What does it mean that 'their god is their belly'? How does heavenly citizenship change how we live on earth?
Application: In what ways are you tempted to set your 'mind on earthly things'? How does the hope of Christ's return and our bodily transformation affect your daily priorities?

subsections.title: Rejoice in the Lord Always
subsections.content: Standing firm, unity, and the peace of God.

questions.question: Context: Who are Euodia and Syntyche (Philippians 4:2-3)? Why does Paul address them specifically in this letter about unity?
Observation: What commands does Paul give (Philippians 4:4-6)? What is the promise in Philippians 4:7? What things should we think about (Philippians 4:8)?
Meaning: How does the command 'do not be anxious' connect to 'prayer and supplication with thanksgiving'? What is the 'peace of God' that guards our hearts and minds?

Application: What are you currently anxious about? Write out a prayer of thanksgiving and supplication about that concern. How can you fill your mind with what is 'true, honorable, just, pure, lovely, and commendable'?

subsections.title: Context for This Week
subsections.content: Paul concludes his letter by thanking the Philippians for their generous gift. In doing so, he reveals the secret of contentment: 'I can do all things through him who strengthens me.' He assures them that God will supply all their needs and closes with greetings and a benediction of grace.

subsections.title: The Secret of Contentment
subsections.content: Learning contentment in every circumstance.

questions.question: Context: What gift had the Philippians sent to Paul? Why had there been a gap in their giving (Philippians 4:10)?
Observation: What has Paul 'learned' (Philippians 4:11-12)? What circumstances does he list? What is the 'secret' he has discovered (Philippians 4:12)?
Meaning: What does 'I can do all things through him who strengthens me' (Philippians 4:13) mean in context? How is this different from a general promise of success in anything we attempt?
Application: Where do you struggle with contentment—in times of plenty or in times of need? How does Christ's strength enable you to be content regardless of circumstances?

subsections.title: God's Provision
subsections.content: Partnership in giving and receiving, and the promise of God's supply.

questions.question: Context: What is unique about the Philippians' partnership with Paul (Philippians 4:15-16)? What does this reveal about their relationship?
Observation: What does Paul seek (Philippians 4:17)? How does he describe their gift (Philippians 4:18)? What does God promise in Philippians 4:19?
Meaning: What does it mean that their gift is 'a fragrant offering, a sacrifice acceptable and pleasing to God'? How does Philippians 4:19 connect to their generosity?
Application: How can you partner in the gospel through your finances and resources? How does the promise of God's provision in Christ Jesus encourage you to give generously?

subsections.title: Final Greetings
subsections.content: Paul's closing greetings and benediction.

questions.question: Context: Who are 'those of Caesar's household' (Philippians 4:22)? How does this connect to Paul's earlier mention of the 'imperial guard' (Philippians 1:13)?
Observation: How does Paul address the recipients? What is his final prayer for them (Philippians 4:23)?
Meaning: Reflect on the entire letter. What are the main themes Paul has emphasized? How do 'joy' and 'Christ' tie everything together?
Application: As you conclude this 6-week study, what is one key truth from Philippians that has impacted you most? How will you live differently because of it?

subsections.title: Study Summary
subsections.content:
Key Themes of Philippians:

  • Joy — Rejoicing regardless of circumstances (1:4, 18; 2:17-18; 3:1; 4:4)
  • Christ-Centered Living — 'To live is Christ' (1:21); knowing Christ as surpassing worth (3:8)
  • Unity & Humility — Having the mind of Christ (2:1-11)
  • Pressing On — The Christian life as a race toward the goal (3:12-14)
  • Contentment — Strength through Christ in all circumstances (4:11-13)
  • Partnership — Sharing in the gospel through relationship and giving (1:5; 4:14-19)

May the grace of the Lord Jesus Christ be with your spirit!
